subject: Regional reserved capacity — mapping, failover, and pricing tradeoffs
messages:
From: Anna Cho <anna.cho@streamline.ai>
To: Sean Gallagher <sean_gallagher@redwood.ai>
Cc: Uday Shah <uday@cloudops.co>
Date: Fri, 09 Oct 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Multi-region reserved capacity questions

Hi Sean —

Thanks for the demo yesterday. We had a good internal sync and Procurement/SRE asked me to follow up with a few concrete questions so we can model cost and contractual language. High level: Streamline is deploying globally with US (primary) and EU (secondary) regions. We expect steady inference traffic for the next 12 months (~120k tokens/min steady, with 3x daily bursts), and we need predictable pricing for capacity planning and compliance reasons.

Can you confirm the following and send a short sketch/estimate?
- Do Reserved/Dedicated pools apply per-region (i.e., separate pools and separate commit charges) or can a single commit be shared across regions?
- If we provision separate pools, what are the replication/DR options and how are they billed (active-active, warm-standby replication, cold DR spin-up)?
- How does cross-region routing for failover affect committed usage? If we route requests to EU from the US pool in failover, does that count against both region commits or only the pool that served the request?
- Minimum throughput guarantees you recommend for a production-grade setup (p95 latency targets: 150–300ms gen, sustained qps targets).

I've attached our capacity_template.csv with expected QPS distribution and region split. Procurement would also like a short Mutual Action Plan (M.A.P) and any sample contract language around failover and burst overage billing.

Anna
Anna Cho | Head of Platform Engineering
Streamline Analytics

From: Sean Gallagher <sean_gallagher@redwood.ai>
To: Anna Cho <anna.cho@streamline.ai>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Dev Patel <dev_patel@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Multi-region reserved capacity questions

Hi Anna —

Appreciate the detail and the template — that helps a lot. Short answers up front, then a pragmatic proposal below.

Quick replies:
- Reserved pools are region-scoped by default (separate pools and separate commit charges). We can support a single logical commitment across regions via an enterprise "pooled commit" add-on but it has tradeoffs (billing complexity and weaker SLA guarantees per region).
- Replication options: active-active (fully provisioned in both regions, higher commit), warm-standby (primary active, secondary kept at a lower reserved level with fast upscaling), cold-DR (no reserved capacity until failover). Billing differs: active-active bills full reserved in both regions; warm-standby bills the smaller reserve in DR + transient burst usage when scaling; cold-DR bills only when capacity is spun up.
- Cross-region routing: charges are applied to the pool that actually serves the request. If the EU pool serves the request, EU reserved capacity is used. If US serves traffic due to failover routing, US pool is charged. The gotcha is cross-region egress and replication transfer costs which we itemize separately.

Pragmatic proposal (based on your CSV):
- Primary (US): commit to a 70% of steady-state tokens. This covers steady QPS and 95th percentile spiky bursts with batching tuned.
- Secondary (EU): warm-standby at ~30% commit with autoscale policy to absorb short failover windows (we recommend a warm-standby target to handle 30–45 minutes of traffic at 1.5x steady QPS).
- Discounting: multi-region combined annual commits qualify for blended discounts; I can sketch scenarios (10–20% band depending on term and commit).
- Throughput guarantees: we can commit to per-pool throughput SLOs (e.g., p95 generation < 300ms for sequences up to 256 tokens) with defined traffic profiles.

I'm attaching a quick sketch (regional_pricing_sketch.pdf) with a couple of commit sizing scenarios and cost deltas for active-active vs warm-standby vs cold-DR. If you want, we can run a short 2-week failover exercise on a reserved dev pool to validate ramp times.

Next steps: if you confirm the preferred failover mode (warm-standby vs active-active), Marissa and I will draft a MAP and a pricing quote, and Dev can produce the autoscaling policy and test plan.

Regards,
Sean

Subject: Re: Multi-region reserved capacity questions

Hi Anna —

Thanks for starting this thread — a couple of commercial notes to make procurement modeling easier:

- Pricing tiers: for annual reserved commits we offer ascending discounts by total commit size. For multi-region deals (two or more region commits combined) we also apply a cross-region stacking discount (typically 5–8 percentage points) because you are consolidating committed spend.
- Replication add-on: warm-standby is an add-on SKU. It is priced as a small percentage of the primary reserve (we typically price it at 25–40% of the full reserve depending on failover SLA). This preserves a predictable committed bill while keeping DR coverage.
- Overages & burst: we offer a capped hourly burst rate and a monthly excess cap to avoid runaway costs in an incident. We can bake simple language into SOW: "burst usage during failover will be billed at on-demand rates beyond reserved capacity, capped at X% of monthly commit unless mutually agreed otherwise."

Commercial offer (initial):
- 12-month combined commit
- 18% blended discount on combined annual committed spend if Streamline signs for both regions together and agrees to a 12-month auto-renewal.
- Warm-standby add-on priced at 30% of primary reserve for DR (applies to EU in your case).

I'll prepare a short MAP + a SOW outline and share the draft SOW_streamline_draft.docx. If procurement has specific contract language requests (e.g., audit rights, data residency clauses), please flag them now so Legal can incorporate.

—Kimberly

Thanks Sean/Kimberly — this is exactly the level of detail Procurement asked for. A few follow-ups from Legal/Procurement:

1) In the warm-standby model, does warm-standby usage (when scaling up during failover) always bill at the warm-standby reserved rate + transient on-demand, or can warm-standby be treated as "free scale" for the first N minutes per incident?
2) For the proposed 18% blended discount and warm-standby priced at 30% of primary — can you show a worked example in dollars for our CSV inputs? Procurement wants an itemized quote that maps to our expected monthly token volumes and burst windows.
3) Contract language: we need explicit failover runbooks and an SLA appendix with escalation contacts and an exercise cadence (we typically ask for semi-annual failover drills).

Separately forwarding Procurement's standard clause for excess usage handling.

Subject: Re: Multi-region reserved capacity questions — proposed structure

Anna/Kimberly —

Thanks for the clarifying questions. Summarizing the recommended commercial and technical structure we will put in the quote and SOW:

1) Architecture & billing model (proposed)\- Separate reserved pools per region (US primary, EU secondary).
\- Warm-standby in EU at 30% of primary reserve; billing for warm-standby is the reserved rate for that allocation.
\- Cross-region requests are billed to the pool that serves the request. During a declared failover incident, we will allow a 20-minute per-incident grace window where failover traffic will not be billed as overage (this is an operational concession we can include in the SOW). After the grace window, transient scale will be billed at on-demand rates until autoscaling finishes to the reserved level.

2) Commit sizing guidance\- Use the provided CSV and the 70/30 split as a starting point. For your numbers, preliminary math: 70% primary commit = ~0.84M committed tokens/day; 30% secondary warm-standby = ~0.36M tokens/day (we will produce exact monthly $ numbers in the quote).

3) Commercials\- 12-month combined commit with an 18% blended discount on annual committed spend.
\- Warm-standby priced at 30% of primary reserve (applies to EU).\- Incident grace: 20 minutes/incident no overage; monthly cap on billed overage will be included (we propose 5% of monthly commit).

4) Ops & SLOs\- We will include a failover appendix: documented runbook, semi-annual failover drills, and a timeline for scale-up (target: DR autoscale to reserved level within 2x of the traffic ramp time, tracked in the appendix).

Next steps: Kimberly/Marissa will craft the MAP and a one-page worked example with dollar figures. Dev will prepare the autoscale policy and a short test plan (2-week validation). I'll circulate a first-pass quote and the SOW by EOD Thurs.

If Procurement is comfortable, can we schedule a 30-minute MAP review Thurs 10/15 at 10am PT?

Thanks,
Sean
